extraction.title: Vitamin C for Preventing and Treating the Common Cold
key_findings: Prophylactic vitamin C supplementation does not reduce the incidence of common colds in the general population, but it significantly reduces incidence by 50% in individuals exposed to extreme physical stress or cold.
Continuous prophylactic use of vitamin C significantly reduces the duration of common cold episodes, by an average of 14% in children and 8% in adults.
Therapeutic use of vitamin C at the onset of cold symptoms generally shows no benefit in reducing cold duration in adults, with one exception of a single 8g dose reducing duration.
The clinical significance of the minor reduction in cold duration during prophylaxis for the general population is questionable, despite indicating a genuine biological effect.
extraction.conclusion: The review concludes that prophylactic vitamin C supplementation does not significantly reduce the incidence of the common cold in normal populations, casting doubt on its widespread utility. While a minor reduction in the duration of cold episodes during prophylaxis was observed, its clinical significance is questionable, despite suggesting a genuine biological effect. However, in special circumstances involving extreme physical exertion and/or cold stress, vitamin C supplementation may offer considerable beneficial effects. Therapeutic use of vitamin C at the onset of symptoms has shown no clear benefits, though further assessment of high-dose single treatments is warranted. The effect of therapeutic vitamin C on children has not yet been examined.
